channel.title: grime95! — one booking a day
channel.description: Serialized small-town fiction: the Ponder County Sheriff's booking records for Saturday, December 2, 1995. One new booking every day at noon Eastern. All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0045 — Nathan Coble: Impersonating Santa Claus (understudy); tractor theft
item.description: Nathan Coble saw a running tractor and a Santa float without a Santa, and figured somebody ought to do something. Nathan is twenty-two, striped shirt, face like a Sunday. Give that boy half a chance to help and he'll help your ass clean into a charge.
item.content:encoded:
Nathan Coble saw a running tractor and a Santa float without a Santa, and figured somebody ought to do something. Nathan is twenty-two, striped shirt, face like a Sunday. Give that boy half a chance to help and he'll help your ass clean into a charge.

The parade had stalled at the Legion. Santa went inside for "one beer," leaving the tractor running and his suit on the seat because the Legion runs hot. Kids waited on the sidewalk. Nathan didn't see a theft. He saw folks fixing to be disappointed.

He put on the suit and drove four blocks down Main to the Pentecostal church, the one Wade Pettibone had rerouted the whole parade around. Idled there twenty minutes, waving and ho ho ho-ing in a voice he later admitted "was mostly Cody Whitlow's dad."

The Pentecostals clapped. Wade was wrong as hell about that.

Real Santa reported the tractor stolen at 9:25. Deputy Hargrove found Nathan passing out candy canes he'd discovered in the float's glove box.

"Step down, Nathan."

"One more block?"

Hargrove gave him one. Damn decent of him, considering he'd have to explain why a stolen tractor got an extension.

In the Polaroid Nathan's still got that little smile. Ain't a lick of bullshit in it. He knows what he did.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0044 — Patsy Delacroix: Disturbing a lawful assembly; assault on a game show host (effigy)
item.description: Patsy Delacroix has watched The Price Is Right every weekday since 1974 and has never been wrong about a showcase. Argue if you want. I'd sooner kick a wasp nest in my church shoes.
item.content:encoded:
Patsy Delacroix has watched The Price Is Right every weekday since 1974 and has never been wrong about a showcase. Argue if you want. I'd sooner kick a wasp nest in my church shoes.

The Legion craft fair opened at nine, in the same hall where the parade had just crashed to a halt. The Methodist men's group had made a life-size plywood Bob Barker for a photo booth. Fifty cents a picture. Patsy paid. Looked at him a good long while.

Wrong hair color. Wrong microphone shape. She told the men they ought to be ashamed of that damn thing, and they laughed. Well, shit. You don't laugh during an inspection.

She knocked his head off with her pocketbook.

“That is not Bob,” she told the Sheriff from a folding chair, red-striped blouse and pink bow, dressed nice for a day nobody had managed to deserve. “You don't get to make a Bob. Especially not that sorry-ass Bob.”

Bless her heart, she'd paid for a picture with somebody she'd eaten lunch with for twenty-one years. They'd handed her lumber with a haircut.

Dwight shot her right there under the BOB BARKER sign, head hanging, jaw set. Come on down. Mind the head.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0043 — Wade Pettibone: Contributing to the delinquency of a minor; parade interference (father)
item.description: Wade Pettibone and his boy Junior got booked together at 9 a.m. and photographed together because Dwight was out of wall. Not film. Wall. That's the kind of Saturday we were having.
item.content:encoded:
Wade Pettibone and his boy Junior got booked together at 9 a.m. and photographed together because Dwight was out of wall. Not film. Wall. That's the kind of Saturday we were having.

Wade is Booster Club clear to the bone. His shirt says CLUB beneath a wildcat that looks like it lost an argument with a grain truck. Arms folded, he told Deputy Hargrove the Christmas parade ought not pass the Pentecostal church because “they don't clap.”

“Band works hard. Least folks could move their damn hands.”

So at 8:50, when the band turned onto Church Street, Wade and Junior blocked the intersection with Wade's Silverado and stood in the bed holding THIS WAY, pointed toward the Legion.

The band followed. They're fifteen-year-olds; give them a sign and they'll follow it plumb into next week. The Shriners followed the band. Santa's tractor followed the Shriners. Whole parade fetched up at the Legion Hall and stopped, because the Legion has a bar. Hell of a navigation aid, a bar.

“Best turnout we ever had,” Wade said.

Can't fault the man's affection for a school band. His judgment's another sack of shit entirely.

Junior smiled for the Polaroid. Wade didn't. Wade knows the routine. Junior's learning it, and apparently driver education comes with matching shirts.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0042 — Josh Wexler: Truancy (Saturday); trespass on school property
item.description: Josh Wexler got picked up for truancy on a Saturday. The Sheriff admitted that was "not a thing," but wrote it down because Josh asked him to. Around here we might could arrest you for something that ain't possible, if you ask decent.
item.content:encoded:
Josh Wexler got picked up for truancy on a Saturday. The Sheriff admitted that was "not a thing," but wrote it down because Josh asked him to. Around here we might could arrest you for something that ain't possible, if you ask decent.

Josh is sixteen, Nike shirt, cap with the green underside showing, face still waiting to see how things turn out. At 8:30 a.m. he was in the high school band room, sitting in the tuba chair and playing nothing. Tyler Nance had the tuba. Tyler was in jail. Whole damn instrument section gone before breakfast.

"I just wanted to see what it felt like," Josh said.

"The chair?"

"Yeah."

Sheriff Ponder had come about the raccoons. He sat in the trombone chair, and neither said anything awhile. Good man. He could spare a kid some quiet; the raccoons could keep tearing up whatever the hell they were tearing up.

Then he said, "Well, you're trespassing."

"Can I be truant instead? It sounds better."

The Sheriff said sure. Trespassing sounds like you're up to some shit. Truant at least suggests somebody expected you.

In the Polaroid Josh has one arm across the frame and his mouth a little open, like he's still in that chair. His mom bailed him out at 9:10, in time to watch the parade go by without a tuba in it.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0041 — Curtis Blevins: Property damage (paint); vandalism of a municipal water tower, attempted
item.description: Before Adam "Double Adam" McCoy set the water tower on fire that night, Curtis Blevins tried to paint it. Adam's got his own entry. One municipal improvement at a time, for hell's sake.
item.content:encoded:
Before Adam "Double Adam" McCoy set the water tower on fire that night, Curtis Blevins tried to paint it. Adam's got his own entry. One municipal improvement at a time, for hell's sake.

Curtis climbed up at dawn with two gallons of white and a roller on a broom handle. He meant to cover PONDER COUNTY and write “something true.” Hadn't settled on what. He was gonna “let the tower tell him.”

Bless his heart, most of us can't get an answer out of the county at ground level.

The tower didn't say shit. The wind, however, had considerable input.

At 8:20 a.m. Deputy Hargrove found Curtis back on the ground, roller in hand, covered head to foot in his own paint. His pink T-shirt had been red an hour earlier. The tower was untouched except for one word he'd managed before the wind turned, eight feet tall: THE.

“THE what, Curtis?”

“I was getting to it.”

“Whole damn town's on the edge of its seat.”

Curtis's eyes are nearly closed in the Polaroid, speckled like a bird's egg. You want to laugh, but the man did climb a water tower for the truth. We mostly just holler for it from a stool.

The THE was still there when the fire started.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0040 — Dallas Yancey: Disorderly conduct; unauthorized Shriner
item.description: Dallas Yancey is twenty, ain't a Shriner, and does not own a fez. He does own a go-kart. At 8 a.m. on parade day he lined up with the Shriners' go-karts in a red puffy coat and purple shirt, figuring the rest might sort itself out.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas Yancey is twenty, ain't a Shriner, and does not own a fez. He does own a go-kart. At 8 a.m. on parade day he lined up with the Shriners' go-karts in a red puffy coat and purple shirt, figuring the rest might sort itself out.

That's a hell of a lot to ask of a puffy coat.

The Shriners looked closely. When the Grand Potentate asked to see his fez, Dallas said it was "in the shop." Asked which shop, he did a lap. Then several more. Boy was trying to outrun a follow-up question at lawnmower speed.

Reserve Deputy Toad stepped in front of the kart with his hand up. Toad directs parade traffic once a year and got deputized by accident in 1988. He trusted that hand more than was sensible.

"Whoa, damn it!"

Toad's fine. He's just slow now. Dallas hadn't meant to hurt a soul; he wanted in the parade so bad he'd forgotten somebody might be standing in it.

In the Polaroid he's hunched and serious under the NO SMOKING sign, the only one all day who looked like he felt bad. He did. Felt like shit, poor kid. Wrote Toad a letter, too. Toad framed it. It's in the hallway.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0039 — Wesley Grimm "Nature Boy": Unlawful release of wildlife (parade); possession of eleven raccoons
item.description: Wesley Grimm called his float “Missouri's Bounty.” Flatbed, hay bales, eleven raccoons in a wire pen. He'd been live-trapping since Halloween. Most folks would've stopped at one raccoon and asked what the hell they were doing.
item.content:encoded:
Wesley Grimm called his float “Missouri's Bounty.” Flatbed, hay bales, eleven raccoons in a wire pen. He'd been live-trapping since Halloween. Most folks would've stopped at one raccoon and asked what the hell they were doing.

The Jaycees told him no Thursday. Wesley showed up anyway in a T-shirt with eagles and a canyon, smiling that little smile of a man who figures permission is mostly for indoor things. God love him, he'd brought the whole damn outdoors.

At 7:55 the Shriners' go-karts fired up behind him in the staging lot. Raccoons don't care for go-karts. Turns out they didn't care for his pen, either.

By the time Deputy Hargrove got the cuffs on, there were raccoons in the Baptist float's manger, in the Sonic Drive-In float's fake tater tots, and on the Jaycees' truck roof. One was inside the tuba Tyler Nance had just been arrested for. That son of a bitch had found the only parade seat with a bell on it.

“They're bounty,” Wesley said. “They'll come back.”

Nine did. Pretty fair return on a wildlife investment, considering the shit he'd put them through.

The calendar behind him in the Polaroid says September 1994. Nothing in this building is current.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0038 — Tyler Nance: Stealing under $150 (one tuba)
item.description: Tyler Nance, fifteen, plays trombone in the Ponder County High School Marching Wildcats. He's wanted the tuba since he was nine, when somebody told him his arms were too short. His arms caught up. The tuba chair didn't. Six years is a hell of a wait for permission to go oom-pah.
item.content:encoded:
Tyler Nance, fifteen, plays trombone in the Ponder County High School Marching Wildcats. He's wanted the tuba since he was nine, when somebody told him his arms were too short. His arms caught up. The tuba chair didn't. Six years is a hell of a wait for permission to go oom-pah.

At 7:30 a.m., ninety minutes before the Christmas parade, Tyler took the tuba.

Didn't hide it. Walked down Main Street carrying the damn thing, which is about as sneaky as stealing a grain bin. He meant to march. That was the whole plan, clear to the fence line.

Deputy Hargrove called it “the most honest thing I saw all day.” Hard to dispute a boy advertising his theft in brass.

In the Polaroid Tyler's grinning, striped button-up on, like he'd ordered this exact Saturday. Behind him is a MIKE KEITH INSURANCE calendar saying November 1994. Nobody in that building flips shit except occasionally their lid.

The band director declined to press charges. Also declined to let him march. Fair enough, but you hate to see a dream get parked indoors.

Tyler played the tuba in the holding cell for an hour. Every note was wrong. Dwight says it was beautiful, and I reckon a man that tired knows joy when it rattles the plumbing.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0037 — Gene Autry Pike "Gene Autry": Animal at large; failure to control livestock (the cow)
item.description: That cow loose on Highway 5 all of December 2, 1995 belonged, on paper, to Gene Autry Pike. Same cow that stopped the donkey, ate the Nativity hay, and walked into the sale barn at midnight like it had called ahead. Busy damn cow.
item.content:encoded:
That cow loose on Highway 5 all of December 2, 1995 belonged, on paper, to Gene Autry Pike. Same cow that stopped the donkey, ate the Nativity hay, and walked into the sale barn at midnight like it had called ahead. Busy damn cow.

Gene Autry said he didn't have one.

Black jacket with racing stripes, cap, head down, half a smile. You know that smile. That's a man whose wife already heard this bullshit and didn't buy any.

"Then whose brand is on it, Gene?"

"Mine. But I sold that cow."

"To who?"

"Myself. Different year."

Now, I like Gene. Most everybody does. But he'd argue with a fencepost and then send the fencepost a bill for standing there.

Sheriff Ponder booked him at seven. Wasn't gonna help a lick, but four calls had come in and the Sheriff needed a name to put on the cow. The cow wasn't offering one. Hell, the cow had places to be.

In the Polaroid there's a fellow asleep at a table behind him. That's Lonnie. He's still there. Between Lonnie and Gene, you had two men available and neither taking responsibility for a hoof.

The cow was never booked. The cow had a better day than anybody.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0036 — Brent Hollis: Theft of services (Walmart layaway line)
item.description: Brent Hollis was seventy-first in the Walmart layaway line at 6:15 a.m. and first at 6:50. Nobody could say exactly how. You'd have thought a man wearing a blue plaid shirt over two other shirts would've been easier to track.
item.content:encoded:
Brent Hollis was seventy-first in the Walmart layaway line at 6:15 a.m. and first at 6:50. Nobody could say exactly how. You'd have thought a man wearing a blue plaid shirt over two other shirts would've been easier to track.

He inched along saying, "'scuse me, my wife's up here," seventy times. Slow. Apologetic. Polite as a church usher moving you away from the good fan.

Brent ain't got a wife. He's got a Super Nintendo on layaway and a nephew he's already told. That's a hell of a promise to make a little boy, and God love him, he meant to keep it. His methods were shit.

The line caught on at the counter. A Missouri line in December has cold feet and a damn good memory. Peg hit him with her purse. A man held his collar till Deputy Stotts arrived, Brent still saying "'scuse me," apparently hoping manners might could reverse a felony.

In the Polaroid he's leaning back, looking serious off to the left, like that whole line's still behind him.

It is. Peg posted his bail so she could stand in front of him again Monday. Woman wasn't finished waiting.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0035 — Kyle Mattingly: Careless driving; failure to secure a load (one Nativity donkey)
item.description: First Baptist rented a donkey for the live Nativity off a man in Lebanon, and Kyle Mattingly got sent to fetch it in his Ranger at 5 a.m., because Kyle is the youth pastor's brother-in-law and that, friends, is how church works.
item.content:encoded:
First Baptist rented a donkey for the live Nativity off a man in Lebanon, and Kyle Mattingly got sent to fetch it in his Ranger at 5 a.m., because Kyle is the youth pastor's brother-in-law and that, friends, is how church works.

Kyle did not bring a trailer. Kyle put a donkey in the bed of a Ford Ranger with a tarp over it and one bungee cord across, and that donkey rode standing up at fifty-five down Highway 5 with its head over the cab like a hood ornament straight out of hell.

The donkey was fine. The donkey, by every account, was having the time of its damn life.

Deputy Hargrove pulled him over at the sale barn, where the loose cow was standing square in the road like it owned the county, and the donkey and the cow looked at each other a good long while, the way two old boys do at a funeral when they ain't sure if they're kin.

"Jesus Christ, Kyle."

"He wanted to see out."

"He's a DONKEY."

"Well, he sure as shit didn't want to see IN."

Kyle's squinting in the Polaroid, blue tee and cap, like a man trying to work out what the charge for a donkey even is. Failure to secure a load. The donkey made the Nativity. Nobody asked how it got there. The cow watched Kyle go, and Hargrove swears it shook its head.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0034 — Randy Culpepper "Sunshine": Public indecency (tanning); operating a tanning bed without a license
item.description: Randy Culpepper bought a tanning bed off a salon in Osage Beach that went under. No salon of his own, no room big enough at the house, so he set it in a horse trailer behind Sunset Lanes and ran an extension cord into the bowling alley's wall. Well, hell. Electricity don't care whether you've got a reception desk.
item.content:encoded:
Randy Culpepper bought a tanning bed off a salon in Osage Beach that went under. No salon of his own, no room big enough at the house, so he set it in a horse trailer behind Sunset Lanes and ran an extension cord into the bowling alley's wall. Well, hell. Electricity don't care whether you've got a reception desk.

He's his own best customer. Look at those shoulders. That ain't a tan you get piddlin' around with yard work.

At 6:10 a.m. Deputy Stotts answered a call about "a blue light and a man's voice going 'ohhh' behind the lanes." She opened the trailer. Randy wore a tank top, a cap, a gold chain, and nothing you'd call pants. Eyes shut. Smiling like the light bill was somebody else's.

"It's for the dance tonight. You can't show up to the VFW pale."

"Randy, it's a horse trailer."

"Horses don't need it. They're outside."

"Your ass is inside, and I can see it from outside."

He didn't let that spoil a damn thing. God love him, all he wanted was to look nice at the dance. Some men buy a shirt; Randy cooks the parts that stick out.

He rode in without opening his eyes. In the Polaroid he still hasn't. Happiest man in the building, no bullshit about it. And he's orange.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0033 — Kayla Sprouse "Miss Ponder County 1995": Theft (one parade float, partial)
item.description: Kayla Sprouse, Miss Ponder County 1995, learned Friday she'd be sharing this year's parade float with Miss Ponder County 1994. That'd be her cousin Brandi. They hadn't spoken since the Fourth of July over a jet ski, and apparently a whole damn float wasn't enough room to continue not speaking.
item.content:encoded:
Kayla Sprouse, Miss Ponder County 1995, learned Friday she'd be sharing this year's parade float with Miss Ponder County 1994. That'd be her cousin Brandi. They hadn't spoken since the Fourth of July over a jet ski, and apparently a whole damn float wasn't enough room to continue not speaking.

At 5:45 a.m. Deputy Hargrove found Kayla in the fairgrounds equipment barn, taking a Sawzall to the float. She'd done the math. Her half had the throne. Brandi's half had opportunities.

Floral blouse, bow off her sash, calm as you please. Most folks look caught when a deputy walks in. Kayla looked like he'd come to help load.

"It's technically my float. The Jaycees gave it to me. I'm giving Brandi some of it."

"You're giving her the trailer hitch, Kayla."

"She can pull."

"How the hell am I supposed to write this up?"

"Put down sharing."

You had to love her nerve. We'd crowned her for poise, and by God, she was keeping her ass poised through a theft investigation.

In the Polaroid she's leaning back, half-lidded, hands folded in her lap, waiting on judges she reckons she can win over. Made bail by 8:30 and rode at nine. Sure as shit, Brandi walked behind carrying the hitch.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0032 — Lonnie Baskett: Sleeping in a public place (Lions Club pancake breakfast, pre-opening)
item.description: The Lions Club found Lonnie Baskett asleep under the griddle at 5:20 a.m. inside the fire station. Padded jacket over a Flintstones T-shirt. Bottle of syrup already open. That boy wasn't leaving a damn thing to chance except waking up.
item.content:encoded:
The Lions Club found Lonnie Baskett asleep under the griddle at 5:20 a.m. inside the fire station. Padded jacket over a Flintstones T-shirt. Bottle of syrup already open. That boy wasn't leaving a damn thing to chance except waking up.

He hadn't broken in. He'd attended the Friday-night fish fry, eaten, and stayed put. The firemen figured he was a Lion. The Lions figured he was a fireman. Everybody turned out the lights. Hell, between two civic organizations you'd think somebody could identify a man full of fish.

"I was first in line," Lonnie told Sheriff Ponder, eyes still shut.

"Lonnie, the line starts outside."

"That's a policy, not a law."

Had him there. Sheriff came for pancakes himself, not a constitutional argument from underneath the cooking equipment.

The Lions were carrying on, so he wrote Lonnie up mostly to hush them, then let him eat first. Decent man. No sense making somebody's breakfast cold just because his ass got there too early.

Lonnie ate eleven. In the Polaroid, taken before a handwritten calendar in the fire chief's office, he's still asleep. Dwight says it's the best one he took all day. Getting a good picture of Lonnie usually involves asking him to quit talking; this was a hell of a shortcut.

Roy Stubblefield's red cap is in the left edge. He was next.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0031 — Roy Stubblefield "Chief": Operating a tree lot without a permit; assault with a Scotch pine
item.description: Roy Stubblefield opened his Christmas tree lot at the old Sinclair station at 5 a.m. He believes people buying trees at 5 a.m. don't haggle. He's right. Anybody shopping for a pine in the dark has other shit going on.
item.content:encoded:
Roy Stubblefield opened his Christmas tree lot at the old Sinclair station at 5 a.m. He believes people buying trees at 5 a.m. don't haggle. He's right. Anybody shopping for a pine in the dark has other shit going on.

Roy had no permit. He had a Chiefs cap, a horseshoe mustache, and a policy. Around here that's most of a business plan.

Deputy Hargrove stopped for a tree. Asked friendly enough to see the permit. Roy asked, considerably less friendly, whether he wanted a tree or a conversation.

"Both."

Roy handed him a seven-foot Scotch pine at a speed the Deputy's report described as "thrown." Hargrove had come intending to spend money with Roy, too. Two fellas trying to have Christmas, and now one had the damn thing coming at his head.

"It's a Christmas tree," Roy said from the back of the cruiser. "You can't assault a man with Christmas."

You sure as hell can. It's needles. The holiday don't round them off.

Dwight shot him under the NO SMOKING sign, serious as a hymn. God love Roy, he looked ready to argue the case clear up to whoever was in charge of pine trees.

His nephew ran the lot the rest of the day and sold out by three. He haggled. Roy's policy wasn't worth a damn without Roy there to throw it.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0030 — Bonnie Threlkeld "Bingo Bonnie": Filing a false report; theft by deception (bingo prizes)
item.description: Bonnie Threlkeld called in the nacho cart theft at 4:20 a.m. and gave particulars fit for a deposition. Tammy Jo Carter had wheeled it out the side door of the bingo hall. True as could be. Bonnie just left out who'd unlocked the door, turned off the alarm, and filled the cart.
item.content:encoded:
Bonnie Threlkeld called in the nacho cart theft at 4:20 a.m. and gave particulars fit for a deposition. Tammy Jo Carter had wheeled it out the side door of the bingo hall. True as could be. Bonnie just left out who'd unlocked the door, turned off the alarm, and filled the cart.

Bonnie had. Woman had done every damn thing but get there first.

She runs Saturday bingo the way Vegas runs Vegas. Six of the last eight blackout jackpots went to her sister, her other sister, and "R. Threlkeld," a man who does not exist. Family resemblance must be hell to establish on that last one.

Deputy Hargrove might've spent all morning sorting it out, except Bonnie, in her floral blouse and big rounded glasses, explaining the theft, said, "before I could get it out myself."

There's your loose board. Stepped right through it.

"Before you could what, Bonnie?"

"Well, shit."

I reckon we've all wished we could reach across a desk and put a sentence back in our mouth. Hers just came with a nacho cart attached.

In the Polaroid her head's tilted. Still figuring whether she actually said that, or whether Hargrove might could have heard some entirely different bullshit.

She said it. When they finally caught Tammy Jo, she called Bonnie "a real one."

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0029 — Jesse Rademacher: Peace disturbance; unlicensed serenade
item.description: Jesse Rademacher stood outside Tammy Jo Carter's trailer at 4:15 a.m., holding a boom box over his head like Cusack. He was playing "The Dance" by Garth Brooks, plaid shirt open to the chest in weather colder than a well-digger's ass.
item.content:encoded:
Jesse Rademacher stood outside Tammy Jo Carter's trailer at 4:15 a.m., holding a boom box over his head like Cusack. He was playing "The Dance" by Garth Brooks, plaid shirt open to the chest in weather colder than a well-digger's ass.

Tammy Jo wasn't home. She was across town stealing a nacho cart from the bingo hall. Jesse had picked a hell of a night to demonstrate how much he could carry.

He serenaded that dark trailer for fifty minutes. Neighbors called at twenty. Deputy Stotts arrived at forty and sat in the cruiser till the song finished. It's a good song. She wasn't about to ruin the only part of this mess that was going right.

"She's not in there, Jesse."

"I know it."

"Then who's the song for?"

He thought on that. "The trailer's heard some things."

Well, shit. You can put a man in a warm car. There ain't a form for the rest of it.

He rode in with the boom box on his lap. In the Polaroid his necklace has a tiny gold nacho pendant. Tammy Jo had it made for him at the county fair in August, before everything went to hell with the cart. Little bitty nacho. He still wore the damn thing right over his heart.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0028 — Travis Oakes: Stealing (one Santa suit); attempted felony chimney entry
item.description: Travis Oakes is nineteen, youngest of eight, and has never gotten what he asked for at Christmas. By the eighth kid, Santa's just dumping whatever's left in the damn sack. This year Travis figured he'd handle distribution himself.
item.content:encoded:
Travis Oakes is nineteen, youngest of eight, and has never gotten what he asked for at Christmas. By the eighth kid, Santa's just dumping whatever's left in the damn sack. This year Travis figured he'd handle distribution himself.

At 4 a.m. they found him on Walmart's roof in a Santa suit he'd shoplifted from that same Walmart Wednesday, halfway into an HVAC duct. He didn't think it was a chimney. Give the boy that much. He thought it went to Electronics.

It went to the deli. Hell of a place to shop for a stereo.

He'd left a note on his Cavalier's windshield: “Gone to work. -T.” Deputy Hargrove considered that a confession. Around here a boy finally shows some initiative and the paperwork eats his ass.

Dwight took the Polaroid at the fingerprint shelf. Striped shirt, forearm on the counter, calm as a fellow waiting on biscuits. Underneath you can see the boot of another guy, asleep, been there since two. God love Travis, he looks willing to wait his turn.

The suit's in evidence. Walmart wants it back. There's a mayonnaise situation. Nobody wants to explain that shit to the returns lady.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0027 — Cody Whitlow: Indecent exposure; attempted baptism without clergy
item.description: Cody Whitlow got saved at 3:30 in the morning, which ain't regular church hours, but Cody wasn't having a regular damn evening. Nobody witnessed it but him. He says that was the point.
item.content:encoded:
Cody Whitlow got saved at 3:30 in the morning, which ain't regular church hours, but Cody wasn't having a regular damn evening. Nobody witnessed it but him. He says that was the point.

He left the Rusty Nail with a clear conscience and a cloudy everything else, walked eleven blocks to First Baptist, and used the side door they never lock because of the Christmas pageant. Climbed into the baptistry in his jeans. Thought on that. Climbed out of his jeans. A man hates to get to heaven in wet denim.

On his fourth full immersion he was telling the ceiling, “I got it, I got it,” when Sheriff Ponder came to check on a light.

“Cody. Son. There's a process.”

“I'm doing the process. Hell, I'm doing it four times.”

“There's a pastor in the process.”

“Well, he ain't here. I am.”

Cody's shirt was never found. The Sheriff brought him in with a choir robe on his lap and the heater going, because salvation is one thing and freezing your ass off is another. God love him, Cody looked relieved enough for both of them.

In the Polaroid he's shirtless, wet-haired, staring straight into the lens. Square with the Lord. Just county bullshit left to handle.

Brother Dale says it counts. He's not happy about it, but it counts.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0026 — Dustin Kroger "Dusty": Vandalism; unlawful posting of bills
item.description: Dusty Kroger walked into the Sheriff's Office at 3:10 a.m. a free man, carrying enough band flyers to correct that oversight. He'd come to bail out his cousin Shane and the deer.
item.content:encoded:
Dusty Kroger walked into the Sheriff's Office at 3:10 a.m. a free man, carrying enough band flyers to correct that oversight. He'd come to bail out his cousin Shane and the deer.

Waiting by the bulletin board, he got bored. In his coat he had flyers for Dusty & the Kroger Brothers, playing the VFW Christmas dance that night. Seemed a shame to waste good wall space on fellas who weren't even coming.

He pinned a flyer over every wanted poster. Neatly, too. Used their own pins. Dusty would never leave you short a pin, bless his heart, even while covering up your whole damn manhunt.

Dwight came back from the Coke machine. Seventeen fugitives had become seventeen Dustys.

"You covered up a murderer, Dusty."

"He's got the whole rest of the state. We got one goddamn dance."

"This ain't a booking agency."

It was fixin' to be one, though.

Dwight booked him right there in his own lobby, navy shirt and mullet and all. The Polaroid shows a Dusty & the Kroger Brothers flyer over his left shoulder. Free publicity, if you weren't particular about the charge underneath.

Shane and the deer waited another four hours. Hell of a favor to do your cousin. The band went on at nine. We love Dusty. They sounded like shit.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0025 — Shane Lockridge: Careless and imprudent driving; transport of a deer, unfield-dressed, in a passenger seat
item.description: Deer camp broke up at midnight, and Shane Lockridge drove home with a ten-point buck riding shotgun, upright, seatbelted, wearing Shane's Cardinals cap. Most folks take home meat. Shane took home somebody to split the driving.
item.content:encoded:
Deer camp broke up at midnight, and Shane Lockridge drove home with a ten-point buck riding shotgun, upright, seatbelted, wearing Shane's Cardinals cap. Most folks take home meat. Shane took home somebody to split the driving.

“For the checkpoint,” he said. There wasn't a damn checkpoint. There was Deputy Hargrove, who stopped him on Highway 5 for doing thirty-one in a fifty-five with his flashers on. That's the speed of a man transporting either dynamite or a covered dish he can't replace.

Shane wore a black tank top in thirty-one-degree weather and a necklace that had belonged to somebody else. God love him, he'd dressed the deer better than himself.

“His name's Gerald. He's seen things.”

“Shane, where the hell is your shirt?”

“Gerald's wearing it.”

Gerald was. Couldn't argue that part. The buck looked ready to help somebody move a couch, except for being dead and full of deer.

Shane's got a little half-smile in the Polaroid. He knows Gerald's still in the truck. He also knows who ain't fixin' to haul that heavy son of a bitch out of there: anybody present.

Nobody did. Gerald sat in impound till Sunday noon, the best-dressed thing in the lot. Shirt, cap, seatbelt. Had his shit together better than most of us.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0024 — Homer Stroud: Misfiled (Henry County, 09 28 96); a future Homer
item.description: The third Henry County photo is dated September 28, 1996. Ten months from now. Well, shit. Most counties can't file yesterday right; this one's already disappointed in next September.
item.content:encoded:
The third Henry County photo is dated September 28, 1996. Ten months from now. Well, shit. Most counties can't file yesterday right; this one's already disappointed in next September.

Homer Stroud. Fifty-some, cap and plaid shirt, two unsmiling views, holding a slate for something he ain't done yet.

Dwight held it up to the cell at 2:40 a.m. "Anybody know a Homer?" Everybody did. Everybody knows a Homer. This particular Homer was the difficulty.

Norman Petrie, Legion adjutant, eating his own raffled ham through the bars, said, "That's Homer Stroud. From Clinton. He does gutters."

"Has he been arrested?"

"Not yet."

"It says September."

Norman studied it. "Well, hell. He's gonna be." Then back to his ham. A man can only worry about so much on an empty fork.

So Homer Stroud does gutters in Clinton, hasn't done whatever he's fixin' to do, and his picture sits in the Ponder County December 2 stack anyhow. God love him, he's getting a head start on a bad day.

The Sheriff called Clinton on Monday, got Homer himself, asked was everything all right. Homer said yes, why. The Sheriff said no reason, hung up, and sat there. What the damn hell do you warn a man against? September?

Dwight says it's the only Polaroid in the stack that's "still developing."

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0023 — Tony Vasquez "Elkins-Swyers": Theft of promotional calendars (34 count)
item.description: Every calendar on every wall of the Ponder County jail says Elkins-Swyers Co. Inc., 1-800-741-0908. Not a damn one says December. Tony Vasquez has supplied the county with all the January it can stand.
item.content:encoded:
Every calendar on every wall of the Ponder County jail says Elkins-Swyers Co. Inc., 1-800-741-0908. Not a damn one says December. Tony Vasquez has supplied the county with all the January it can stand.

Tony drives for Elkins-Swyers. Back in January somebody told him to get the calendars out, and he took that to heart. Bars, church basements, sheriff's offices. God love him, the man distributed time like folks were fixin' to run short.

Come December he still had thirty-four in the truck. Thirty-four was enough to get asked about. Tony wasn't scared of work; he was scared of standing by a desk while somebody counted shit.

At 2:30 a.m. Deputy Hargrove found him behind the Elkins-Swyers warehouse, feeding the leftovers back through a window. Salmon-striped shirt over a teal tee. Dressed for a vacation, working a reverse burglary.

"Tony, what the hell are you doing?"

"They're not stolen, they're unreturned."

"You're putting them in."

"Well, I ain't gonna fix it taking more out."

Hard to fault that part. The rest was bullshit, but that part stood up real good.

Dwight shot the Polaroid in front of one of the calendars. January 1995. Tony did not look at it. He'd already had that month up to here.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0022 — Lamar Quisenberry: Misfiled (Henry County); monochrome; possibly not a person
item.description: The second Henry County photo is blue all over. Front and profile, mullet, raglan shirt, slate. Whatever camera took it made the whole works underwater green-blue. Poor fella looks like somebody already remembers him wrong.
item.content:encoded:
The second Henry County photo is blue all over. Front and profile, mullet, raglan shirt, slate. Whatever camera took it made the whole works underwater green-blue. Poor fella looks like somebody already remembers him wrong.

The slate says Lamar Quisenberry. Or Dwight read Lamar Quisenberry at 2:35 in the morning and wrote it down. At that hour your name's whatever the awake man can spell. Be grateful it ain't “goddamn blur.”

Nobody's claimed him. Henry County says no. Ponder County says no. Lamar, wherever and whenever he is, hasn't weighed in. Reckon he might like a vote.

Louella Fenwick studied the photo through the bars.

“Oh, that's Verle's cousin's boy.”

Looked again. “No it isn't.”

Third look. “Well, it might be.”

That's the closest we got. Three identifications, all from one woman, and none worth a shit in court.

He's unsmiling both ways, holding the slate like he's held one before. There's a longer story somewhere, some year, some county with a working camera. Ain't a bit of it here.

Dwight put him between a Santa and a Chiefs fan anyway. Decent enough company for a man nobody can place. By 2:35 a.m. the record had quit being about who did what. Hell, we were past that.

It's about who was in the pile. Lamar's in the pile.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0021 — Ned Arbogast: Filed under the wrong county (Henry); wrong year; charge unknown
item.description: At 2:30 a.m., forty-eight Polaroids into the Rexall Spectra, Dwight found a manila envelope under the booking desk: HENRY COUNTY -- RETURN. Four proper booking photos inside, front and profile, black slate, state camera. County south of here. Dates scattered through 1996, which hadn't happened yet.
item.content:encoded:
At 2:30 a.m., forty-eight Polaroids into the Rexall Spectra, Dwight found a manila envelope under the booking desk: HENRY COUNTY -- RETURN. Four proper booking photos inside, front and profile, black slate, state camera. County south of here. Dates scattered through 1996, which hadn't happened yet.

He put them in the stack. Hell, why let the calendar get bossy now?

Says it was an accident. Says he was tired. Says a picture's a picture. Here comes Ned Arbogast, plaid over teal, hair retreating hard, holding HENRY COUNTY SHERIFF DEPT 03 30 96 like somebody asked him to and he'd rather not prolong the discussion.

Nobody in Ponder County knows Ned Arbogast. Nobody here's been to Henry County on purpose. Monday the Sheriff called. They'd never heard of Ned either, hadn't sent an envelope, and wanted to know what year it was. Damn good question. Wrong office to ask.

Ned ain't in the cell. Never was. He's between Jo Bob Sackett and a woman with a cup in the stack, serious, sideways and then forward, from a March that hasn't come, in a county denying custody of his very existence. He'll be there forever. That's some durable clerical bullshit.

Dwight says he looks “like he belongs.”

He does. Everybody does by now. Don't know the fellow, but there's room for his picture.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0020 — Jo Bob Sackett "Santa": Photographed with the wrong slate; identity disputed
item.description: Jo Bob Sackett is the only man in the whole Polaroid run holding a booking slate. Brought his own. County service had got so poor even Santa was supplying materials.
item.content:encoded:
Jo Bob Sackett is the only man in the whole Polaroid run holding a booking slate. Brought his own. County service had got so poor even Santa was supplying materials.

The real Santa. Parade Santa. Went into the Legion for one beer at 9:20 that morning and came out to Nathan Coble driving his float to the Pentecostals in his suit. Jo Bob spent the day hunting suit, float, tractor, and eventually Larry Boggs, who'd driven the whole mess to his mother's. By 2 a.m. he'd found none of it. Came to jail to report himself.

"As what?" Dwight asked.

"Missing."

"You're right damn here."

"That's what missing people always say."

Hell, try arguing with that after the day Dwight had. Jo Bob's slate was a shoebox lid: JO BOB in Sharpie, SANTA underneath, then ASK, smaller. Black shirt, white beard, wristwatch. Not smiling. Most convincing Santa in the county, and somebody else had his pants.

"You can't file yourself missing, Jo Bob."

"Lacey Harmon did."

Another point. Everybody had a point today and nobody had a goddamn solution. Dwight shot him holding the slate.

He's in the cell. The suit's in evidence with the mayonnaise. Nathan Coble apologized. Jo Bob said the kid did fine. That's our Santa: day ruined, still making sure the boy knows he ain't.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0019 — Louella Fenwick: Public intoxication; unlawful use of a church bell
item.description: First Methodist rang forty-one times at two in the morning. Sheriff Ponder counted every damn one before he got dressed. You give a church bell that much rope, you generally ain't announcing a bake sale.
item.content:encoded:
First Methodist rang forty-one times at two in the morning. Sheriff Ponder counted every damn one before he got dressed. You give a church bell that much rope, you generally ain't announcing a bake sale.

Louella Fenwick was up in the tower wearing her cream blouse and one shoe, with most of a bottle of Boone's Farm. She held the rope like she was waiting on a bus that ought to know better by now.

“How many is that?”

“Forty-one.”

“I was married forty-one years, Marvin.” She pulled again. “Forty-two.”

Well, hell. The Sheriff sat on the tower steps. He'd known Louella since fourth grade and her husband Verle since third. Verle was buried the Tuesday before Thanksgiving. You can look through that whole statute book and not find what to do with a woman who's still got years to count and nobody to count them with.

He let her get to fifty. Didn't hurry her a bit. Then he drove her in, and Dwight took the Polaroid: chin down, one hand curled at her chest, holding nothing.

Nobody filed the damn paperwork. The Methodists changed the lock.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0018 — Deborah Kincaid "The Realtor": Trespass; attempted showing of an occupied residence
item.description: Deborah Kincaid sold four houses in 1995 and has never once slept through the night. Some folks count sheep. Deborah probably wonders what the damn pasture would appraise for.
item.content:encoded:
Deborah Kincaid sold four houses in 1995 and has never once slept through the night. Some folks count sheep. Deborah probably wonders what the damn pasture would appraise for.

At 1:40 a.m. she let herself into 412 Poplar with a lockbox key, herringbone coat over a red top, and commenced selling the crown molding to a couple she'd collected in the Rusty Nail parking lot. They weren't buyers. They were drunk. The house wasn't for sale, and the Hendersons were asleep upstairs, enjoying what they thought was ownership.

“Original hardwoods,” Deborah said when Mr. Henderson came down with a bat.

She handed him a card. God love her, a man could come downstairs carrying hell on a stick and she'd see a referral.

Deputy Stotts found the couple in the kitchen eating the Hendersons' pie and Deborah measuring the master closet.

“Deborah, these people live here.”

“Well, sure. Shows the place works.”

She went quietly. Ain't a mean bone in her; just no off switch anybody's located. Her eyes are nearly closed in the Polaroid. Not shame. She hasn't slept since the Tuesday after Labor Day, and shit, that'd make anybody confuse a felony with an open house.

The Hendersons have listed the house. With her.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0017 — Jordan Pettis: Interfering with a jailer (haircut, unsolicited, on Dwight)
item.description: Misty Rawlins did forty heads of hair through the cell bars with an Avon comb between 6:45 and 9, and got out at ten, and left the comb, and at 1:30 a.m. Jordan Pettis -- twenty-six, mint-green tank top in December, not a hairdresser but has "watched" -- picked it up.
item.content:encoded:
Misty Rawlins did forty heads of hair through the cell bars with an Avon comb between 6:45 and 9, and got out at ten, and left the comb, and at 1:30 a.m. Jordan Pettis -- twenty-six, mint-green tank top in December, not a hairdresser but has "watched" -- picked it up.

He didn't go for the cell, the sneaky son of a bitch. The cell was done. He went for Dwight.

Dwight was asleep. Sitting up at the counter, head down, the stolen Spectra in front of him, out cold for the first time since Friday. And Jordan stood behind him with that comb and looked at Dwight's hair, which lives under a ZEBCO cap at all times and had not been seen by living eyes in years, and lifted the cap.

He got about four minutes in before the Sheriff came out of his office and stopped dead.

"Jordan."

"Shh."

"What in the goddamn --"

"He's had a DAY, Marvin. Look at him. Man's been rode hard and put up wet since Friday. Let me do this one thing."

The Sheriff looked. Dwight, asleep, his hair -- Lord, there's more of it than anybody thought -- being combed real gentle by a man in a tank top at two in the morning, and the Sheriff, who is not a soft man but has his moments, said, quiet, "Finish, then," and Jordan did.

He's got his arms behind his back in the Polaroid, serious, like a man who's done something he can't undo and wouldn't if he could. Dwight woke up at three with a part. He kept it. Nobody's said a damn word. Everybody's noticed. Hailey says he looks like a weatherman.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0016 — Harlan Peavey: Receiving stolen property (one prosthetic leg)
item.description: When Deputy Hargrove raided the Legion men's-room casino, Ricky "Vegas" Lankford went to collect the leg he'd won at poker. Too late. That son of a bitch had walked off without its owner, under Harlan Peavey's arm.
item.content:encoded:
When Deputy Hargrove raided the Legion men's-room casino, Ricky "Vegas" Lankford went to collect the leg he'd won at poker. Too late. That son of a bitch had walked off without its owner, under Harlan Peavey's arm.

Harlan is a tan-shirt, side-part, Sunday-school man and the Legion treasurer. God love him, he could make stealing sound like something you needed a quorum for.

"I'm securing club assets."

"It ain't a club asset, Harlan. It's Delbert's damn leg."

"Delbert put it in the pot."

There was the trouble. Harlan wasn't disputing whose leg it was. He was disputing which column it belonged in.

At 1:30 a.m. they picked him up in the Legion parking lot, trying to fit it in a Buick trunk already full of bingo cages. Hell of a place to store a lower extremity, but the treasurer hadn't asked us. He kept saying "now hold on," polite as could be, like Hargrove was fixin' to approve last month's minutes without reading them.

In the Polaroid his arms stick out like he's still carrying it. Poor fellow looks ready to receive another donation. Delbert got the leg back Monday. Says it's been in a Buick; he can tell.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0015 — Sal Bianchi: Running a book (on the cow)
item.description: Sal Bianchi gave a cow forty-to-one odds on going home, and now he owed a woman in jail two hundred dollars. That's a hell of a way to learn livestock.
item.content:encoded:
Sal Bianchi gave a cow forty-to-one odds on going home, and now he owed a woman in jail two hundred dollars. That's a hell of a way to learn livestock.

He'd been taking bets since ten that morning. Where it'd be at noon. Whether it'd make the Nativity. Whether Duane Fenster would hit it, long odds, correctly. Caught by dark? By nine? By midnight? He offered forty to one on it walking into the sale barn on its own, for a joke.

Louella Fenwick put five dollars on that, from the cell, by phone, through Lyle Tackett's taxi. Damn cow walked into the sale barn on its own at ten.

At 1 a.m. Sal was at the Spur, book open on the bar, trying to figure out paying a woman in jail. Black-and-burgundy shirt, mustache, head tilted. You could about hear the arithmetic hurting.

"Sal, that's a book."

"It's a notebook."

"It says 'COW' on the cover and it's got odds in it."

"Everybody had a piece of that cow, Lula Mae."

Everybody did. She booked him. He asked for the cell so he could pay Louella in person. No bullshit about waiting till payday, either. God love Sal, he might price a cow wrong, but he paid cash.

Louella gave him twenty back. "For the trouble." The whole cell watched like it was a wedding. Subdued in the Polaroid. Broke. Honest about it. The cow never knew.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0014 — Carla Beeson: Unlawful entry; impersonating a health inspector
item.description: Carla Beeson went through the Hardee's drive-thru at 12:50 a.m., ordered a Frisco burger, and got told the grill was down. Most folks would've gone home hungry. Carla said, "Then I'll need to see the grill." Like the damn thing was on her insurance.
item.content:encoded:
Carla Beeson went through the Hardee's drive-thru at 12:50 a.m., ordered a Frisco burger, and got told the grill was down. Most folks would've gone home hungry. Carla said, "Then I'll need to see the grill." Like the damn thing was on her insurance.

She parked, went through the employee door, and started opening reach-in coolers in oversized tinted glasses and her mother's plaid blouse. Wrote on a napkin. Said "mm-hm" with enough disappointment to make two employees start cleaning. Hell, that blouse alone could've made a boy wipe a counter.

The night manager, nineteen-year-old Colton, asked for credentials. Carla showed him a Blockbuster card. Bless her heart, she had identification. It just identified somebody who could rent a movie.

"That's when I called," Colton told Deputy Stotts. "It was more the confidence than the card."

"You did fine, hon. Hard to argue with a woman already writing your shit down."

In the Polaroid Carla's hunched, lips parted, fixin' to declare the fryer oil a violation. It was. Nobody wrote it down. She'd come for supper and nearly improved the place.

The grill's still down.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0013 — Mason Ealy: Vandalism (courthouse star, attempted improvement, with a ladder)
item.description: Mason Ealy went after the courthouse flicker with a screwdriver and no particular way of reaching it. Fifteen years old. Bless his heart, at that age a ladder feels like most of a plan.
item.content:encoded:
Mason Ealy went after the courthouse flicker with a screwdriver and no particular way of reaching it. Fifteen years old. Bless his heart, at that age a ladder feels like most of a plan.

Chuck Ledbetter lit the courthouse star at 10:25 using a bucket truck he wasn't supposed to have. Grounded wrong, Manny Ortega said from the cell. At 12:40 a.m. Mason figured he might could fix it.

Fetched a ladder from the Rexall's alley. Got about a third of the way up the courthouse. What was he aiming to do at the top? Hadn't worked that part out. He admitted to "a screwdriver and a feeling."

Gus Halloran, still on the steps under the star in his orange, watched him climb.

"Son, you ain't gonna reach it."

"I know."

"Then what are you doing?"

"Trying."

Gus said okay and watched. Can't hardly fault the trying, though somebody ought to check the ladder.

Deputy Stotts came back from the bell tower with Toby Rasmussen and found a fifteen-year-old up against the courthouse and an escaped prisoner spotting him. She stopped. Stood there a spell. Then walked over and held the ladder herself while Mason came down. No sense scaring the boy into falling.

He's leaning right in the Polaroid, mouth open a little in a smile, blue tee with cursive on it. Curfew. Gus went back in with him. The star still flickers. It's kind of nice. Nobody says so.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0012 — Marcus Tillery "Monday Night": Assault with a fowl; disturbing the peace
item.description: Marcus Tillery has worn the same Monday Night Football polo to the Rusty Nail every Saturday since 1989, on the theory that it confuses God. It has not confused God. It has confused a good many bartenders.
item.content:encoded:
Marcus Tillery has worn the same Monday Night Football polo to the Rusty Nail every Saturday since 1989, on the theory that it confuses God. It has not confused God. It has confused a good many bartenders.

At 12:20 a.m. some jackass from Camdenton announced Nebraska would beat Florida by forty. Marcus had no dog in that fight and had never been within four hundred miles of Nebraska, but he'd won a frozen Butterball at the Legion turkey shoot and had been toting it around like a football for six hours, waiting on a reason.

"It was a hand-off," he told Deputy Stotts. "He just didn't have his goddamn hands ready."

The Camdenton fella lost a tooth. The turkey lost nothing. It is still froze solid. It is in evidence, in the break-room fridge, next to Hargrove's yogurt.

Dwight shot the Polaroid by the Coke machine because the real booking camera's been dead since Thanksgiving. Marcus stood there calm as a deacon at a funeral he didn't much care about and asked, polite as you please, if he might could get the turkey back by Christmas.

Dwight said that depended on the turkey.

Marcus said, "Well, hell, it ain't going anywhere." God love him, he's right. It's still in there.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0011 — Toby Rasmussen: Disturbing the peace (church bell, second ringing)
item.description: The Methodists changed the bell-tower lock at noon after Louella Fenwick rang it fifty times at two in the morning for Verle. Left the key on a nail by the door. Well, hell. You can buy hardware; you can't buy suspicion.
item.content:encoded:
The Methodists changed the bell-tower lock at noon after Louella Fenwick rang it fifty times at two in the morning for Verle. Left the key on a nail by the door. Well, hell. You can buy hardware; you can't buy suspicion.

By half past midnight Toby Rasmussen was up there. Twenty-four, dirty-blond, sale-barn hand. He'd spent the day chasing the cow, same as Jason Kimbrough, with the same damn results everybody got. Came to the Nail at ten and heard about Louella.

He rang eleven times.

"Eleven?" Deputy Stotts stood at the top of the stairs, out of breath again. Those steps hadn't got any shorter since her last trip.

"I've had eleven beers."

"That's not what she was doing, Toby."

"I know what she was doing." He rang again. Twelve. "That's for Verle. The other eleven were for me."

Stotts sat on the step, the second deputy today to park there. Reckon she could spare him a little time. She let him get to fifteen.

"That's plenty, hon."

He agreed. Coming down, he asked whether Louella was still in. Yes. Could he be put in with her?

"It's one cell, Toby. Everybody's in with her. Ain't a goddamn hotel."

He's startled in the Polaroid, lips parted, cream tee, looking like nobody mentioned the flash. Louella patted the bench. He sat. Neither said a word. The bell's got a new lock. Key's on the nail.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0010 — Rusty Jane Walker: Booked by wager; no charges filed
item.description: When Rusty Jane Walker walked into the county fair's chili cook-off, there was no mistaking her presence. With her hair permed into a mullet sharp enough to cut steel and a pair of denim overalls that looked like they’d been through more wars than peace treaties, she became an instant conversation starter—and ender. The overalls weren’t just her statement piece; they were her armor.
item.content:encoded:
When Rusty Jane Walker walked into the county fair's chili cook-off, there was no mistaking her presence. With her hair permed into a mullet sharp enough to cut steel and a pair of denim overalls that looked like they’d been through more wars than peace treaties, she became an instant conversation starter—and ender. The overalls weren’t just her statement piece; they were her armor.

Rusty Jane had a knack for two things: out-eating anyone dumb enough to challenge her, and scaring off barflies with her thousand-yard stare. It was said she once stared down a runaway bull, and the bull apologized. But tonight wasn’t about livestock or looks—it was about chili, and Rusty Jane's concoction, “Fire in the Hole,” had earned her three consecutive first-place ribbons.

Except this year, Old Man Tugger decided to wager big against her. Tugger, with his "secret family recipe" (rumored to include wild mushrooms and a splash of moonshine), had upped the stakes: the loser had to pose for a mugshot in front of the fair’s fake county jail—an embarrassing rite of passage.

Rusty Jane didn't bat an eyelash. “Tugger,” she drawled, her voice lower than most men’s, “if I lose, I’ll even let you slap my mugshot on the billboard down Route 12.”

The contest was tight. Tugger’s chili made a judge cry actual tears, but Rusty Jane’s lit a fire in their souls. The deciding factor? A random carnie running through the fairgrounds screaming, "Tugger used canned beans!" Rusty Jane leaned back in her chair and roared with laughter as Tugger was dragged, fuming, to the photo booth.

Rusty Jane, ever the crowd-pleaser, stepped into the booth too. "Take one for the fans," she told the photographer, deadpan. And thus, the legend of Rusty Jane’s mugshot was born.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0009 — Buck McGraw "Honest Buck": Theft of fuel from a county vehicle
item.description: The thing about “Honest Buck” McGraw is that nobody believes he’s honest, least of all himself. By the time he rolled into the station tonight smelling like diesel fuel, he was already two steps into trouble.
item.content:encoded:
The thing about “Honest Buck” McGraw is that nobody believes he’s honest, least of all himself. By the time he rolled into the station tonight smelling like diesel fuel, he was already two steps into trouble.

Buck had been drinking in a booth at the Rusty Spur, scribbling poetry about "the beauty of oil stains on asphalt." By his third bourbon, the poem had somehow turned into a plan. Ten minutes later, he was sprawled under the sheriff’s cruiser in the parking lot, mouth-siphoning gasoline with the kind of passion usually reserved for true love or last rites.

When they dragged him in, still coughing up fumes, Buck just grinned through bloodied teeth. “A man’s gotta keep the engine running,” he slurred.

The mugshot shows him defiant, shirt stained with whiskey and grease, eyes daring the camera to blink first. Somewhere in the background, you can almost hear him mutter: “They’re gonna call this art one day.”

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0008 — Gary Wayne Mullins: Negligent operation of a motor vehicle
item.description: Gary Wayne Mullins had one talent: falling asleep in the worst possible moments.
item.content:encoded:
Gary Wayne Mullins had one talent: falling asleep in the worst possible moments.

“Gary, wake up!” Sheriff Ponder banged the table. “You’re in jail, for Pete’s sake!”

Gary’s head jerked up. “Huh? Where am I?”

Deputy Hargrove shook his head. “You fell asleep at the gas station… again. Truck running, gear in neutral. Rolled straight into the donut rack.”

Gary winced. “Was anyone hurt?”

“Only the powdered donuts. Whole shelf toppled. Brenda Sue’s still sweeping up sugar.”

Gary nodded solemnly. “Reckon I should apologize.”

“Reckon you should stop napping in public places,” Ponder snapped. “Last week, it was the hardware store. Before that, the post office. I’m out of patience.”

Gary yawned. “Well, jail’s quiet. Can I catch a nap now?”

“You’re bonded out already,” Hargrove said. “Tammy Jo paid it.”

Gary scratched his head. “Tammy Jo? Why?”

“Don’t ask us,” Hargrove muttered. “She just said you’re ‘good for a laugh.’”

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0007 — Tammy Jo Carter: Grand theft cart; vandalism; release of livestock
item.description: Tammy Jo Carter sat in the holding room, her sweater pristine despite the chaos she’d caused.
item.content:encoded:
Tammy Jo Carter sat in the holding room, her sweater pristine despite the chaos she’d caused.

“So,” began Deputy Hargrove, holding back a grin. “You stole Billy Ray’s nacho cart and drove it into the gazebo?”

Tammy Jo nodded, unbothered. “It was blocking the bingo hall. The ladies were restless.”

“And the spray paint?”

“‘No nachos on bingo night’ felt appropriate.”

“And why’d you release Earl’s pet pig into the bakery?”

Tammy Jo shrugged. “Earl bet me twenty bucks I wouldn’t.”

Sheriff Ponder pinched his nose. “Tammy Jo, do you have any idea how much damage you’ve done tonight?”

“Not as much as Double Adam or Earl,” she said sweetly.

Ponder sighed. “You bonded out yet?”

“Already done,” she replied, smug. “Same as every Friday.”

Tammy Jo was a local legend—her crimes were always petty, but her timing impeccable.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0006 — Adam McCoy "Double Adam": Grand theft ornament; arson; unauthorized use of a vehicle
item.description: “Double Adam” McCoy tilted his head at the camera, his two Adam’s apples twitching as he swallowed. His aviators hid bloodshot eyes, and his plaid shirt was shredded like it had been through a combine.
item.content:encoded:
“Double Adam” McCoy tilted his head at the camera, his two Adam’s apples twitching as he swallowed. His aviators hid bloodshot eyes, and his plaid shirt was shredded like it had been through a combine.

“Double Adam,” Sheriff Ponder sighed. “What in God’s name possessed you to lasso the town’s Christmas angel off the water tower?”

Adam smirked. “Needed a mascot for the demolition derby.”

“The derby that wasn’t even scheduled?”

“Sometimes life don’t wait for paperwork, Sheriff.”

Ponder gestured to his burnt boots. “And the fireworks?”

“Spirited things up. Until the angel caught fire.”

“And the truck you flipped into the creek?”

“Borrowed it. Temporarily. Technically, I was done with it by then.”

Ponder glared. “You know Billy Ray’s nacho cart floated downriver, right?”

Adam shrugged. “He should thank me. Free advertising.”

As Ponder cuffed him, Adam grinned. “Ain’t this town fun on Friday nights?”

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0005 — Billy Ray Thornton: Disorderly conduct; assault with currency
item.description: Billy Ray Thornton (no relation) adjusted his crooked yellow aviators and sighed as the bondsman snapped his photo.
item.content:encoded:
Billy Ray Thornton (no relation) adjusted his crooked yellow aviators and sighed as the bondsman snapped his photo.

“So, Billy Ray,” the bondsman smirked, “what’d you do this time?”

Billy Ray scratched his beard, the faint smell of chili still clinging to him. “Well, it all started when Earl Griggs bet me I couldn’t eat six chili cheese dogs and bowl a perfect game.”

The bondsman raised an eyebrow. “And?”

“I got to four dogs before I blacked out. Woke up at the bowling alley snack bar with a corndog in one hand and a pile of nickels in the other.”

Sheriff Ponder’s voice barked from across the room. “Tell him the rest, Billy Ray.”

He winced. “Apparently, I decided to start payin’ for nachos by chuckin’ nickels at the shoe rental guy. He wasn’t impressed.”

The bondsman laughed. “And Earl?”

Billy Ray shook his head. “He’s back in lockup for some kinda vending machine rescue mission.”

Sheriff Ponder groaned, grabbing more paperwork. “This whole town’s lost its mind tonight.”

Billy Ray grinned. “Nah, Sheriff. We’re just warmin’ up.”

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0004 — Earl Griggs "Smokey": Public intoxication; indecent exposure; destruction of property
item.description: Earl "Smokey" Griggs stumbled out of the county jail, his breath reeking of stale beer and bad decisions. Darla Mae, his long-suffering sister, leaned against her Buick, arms crossed.
item.content:encoded:
Earl "Smokey" Griggs stumbled out of the county jail, his breath reeking of stale beer and bad decisions. Darla Mae, his long-suffering sister, leaned against her Buick, arms crossed.

“What now, Earl?” she snapped as he climbed in.

He burped and slurred, “Ain’t my fault this time, Darla. The jukebox at The Rusty Nail was playin’ my song, and I just… got inspired.”

Darla glared. “Inspired to ride the mechanical bull naked?”

Earl grinned. “I thought it’d be funny!”

“It wasn’t funny when you knocked over three tables and scared the Johnsons’ Pomeranian into the dartboard!”

Earl shrugged. “Sheriff Ponder overreacted. A man’s got a right to have fun.”

“You puked in her hat, Earl.”

He squinted. “That’s what that was?”

As Darla drove home, Earl passed out mid-mutter, while she muttered prayers that he’d someday sober up—or at least run out of bars to get banned from.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0003 — Norma June Wiley "Miss Twirl 1973": Criminal trespass; resisting
item.description: Norma June Wiley never actually opened her eyes the entire time she was in custody.
item.content:encoded:
Norma June Wiley never actually opened her eyes the entire time she was in custody.

She was found in the high school gym, passed out in the trophy case, clutching a glittery baton and whispering, “Miss Twirl 1973 never dies.”

When asked how she got in, she said she had “unfinished business” with the pep band. No one could confirm what that meant, but a flute was missing, and the janitor’s bucket was full of peppermint Schnapps.

Deputies said she briefly fought them off using only her elbow and an empty lipstick tube.

She finally bonded out when her ex-husband’s cousin recognized her and muttered, “Ah hell, not again.”

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0002 — Floyd Danner: Aggressive loitering; unauthorized sandwich distribution
item.description: Floyd Danner got picked up at precisely 5:47 p.m., halfway through his fourth Schlitz and mid-lecture on “the sacred geometry of horseshoe pits.”
item.content:encoded:
Floyd Danner got picked up at precisely 5:47 p.m., halfway through his fourth Schlitz and mid-lecture on “the sacred geometry of horseshoe pits.”

According to the report, Floyd was arrested for “aggressive loitering and unauthorized sandwich distribution” after setting up a card table in front of the DMV and trying to sell baloney sandwiches wrapped in used napkins.

He told the deputy, “I’m providing a service, son. You ever sat through a title transfer sober?”

When they took his mugshot, Floyd leaned in and asked, “Is this going in the Newsletter? ’Cause I want my good side.”

He doesn’t have a good side.

All persons and events are fiction.

item.title: 95-12-0001 — Ricky Lankford "Vegas": Operating an unlicensed gaming establishment
item.description: They call him “Vegas” because he once spent 11 hours at the slots in Tunica and came home with nothing but a divorce and a ferret named Chaz.
item.content:encoded:
They call him “Vegas” because he once spent 11 hours at the slots in Tunica and came home with nothing but a divorce and a ferret named Chaz.

On Dec. 2, 1995, Ricky Lankford got pinched for running a “pop-up casino” in the American Legion men’s room.

The poker game was going fine until someone bet their prosthetic leg, and Ricky tried to collect.

“Legs is currency if there’s a buy-in,” he argued, shirt half-tucked, gold chain flashing under that tragic candy-stripe button-down.

The mugshot was snapped minutes after Deputy Hargrove forced Ricky to empty his pockets—six dice, a crumpled Polaroid of his ex-wife, and $14 in loose change.

He left with a warning and a limp. Not his.

All persons and events are fiction.
